I like the Singapore model. I think it sounds good. I think we should explore it. But I think in general, there’s just so little policy ideation in this space because everyone’s just bought into this forced saving model as the only way to get people to...

Matthew Yglesias: …so let me put out some other ideas. Like, somebody should try to create, like, the government, you know, maybe not as a direct sale, but right, there should be some form of, like, rent insurance that people can purchase, right? That will, like, hedge against your rent going up.

Because, like, a lot of this rent control discourse is, I think people are, like, correctly saying that there’s, like, an actual tangible value to security of tenure in a given spot. And then, they’re trying to create that through a way that has, like, massive costs to society. But, like, there could be a way to create that for people that is not as, like, socially destructive, right?

I think we agree, like, it should be allowed to build apartment buildings in more places. It also shouldn’t be, like, a special regulatory prohibition on renting a house, which is, like, a very odd idea that has become mainstream in American politics. We should do something to make regular savings simpler.

But I don’t know — I don’t know how much difference any of that makes, ultimately, to this question of, like, whether people want to own homes, unless we want to do something that I would not favor, which is, like, cutting off the government sponsorship of mortgages.

Because I think that’s the crux point. Back when I was a true, “the homeownership society is a cancer”-kind of person, I was like, we got to get rid of the 30-year mortgage. We got to get rid of Fannie and Freddie. We got to get rid of these tax benefits.

And now I’m much more like, “People are going to hate that and it’s not going to have any real benefit.”

Jerusalem Demsas: So, I like this idea a lot. I know there’s an econ paper. I was trying to find it. There’s an econ paper that someone proposed this. I think Han-Suck Song, is it? Is that what you were thinking of? Insurance against rent increases?

Matthew Yglesias: Oh, I don’t know. I thought I just made this up.

Jerusalem Demsas: No, sir. You did not make this up. But it’s a great idea. Maybe you’re the Leibniz to this guy’s Newton.

So, anyway, but yeah, basically in this situation, the insurance would function as a call option, giving the tenant the right to stay in their apartment, paying the lower of the current market rent or the contractually fixed strike rent with the landlord acting as the insurer. That’s his model. It’s basically just a paper. No one’s actually done this.

I think this is, like, I think this is a really good idea, but I mean, I think getting, like, going back to, like, what problem we’re actually solving here. I am, like, actually really comfortable with homeownership as consumption.

And, to be clear, before we saw these, like, massive amounts of appreciation in certain parts of the country, particularly in, like, you know, post-1970s anti-growth regime, people didn’t really expect their homes to appreciate, like, 7% a year. Like, that was, like, was not, like, normal. You’d, like, imagine, like, maybe you would match, like, the cost-of-living rises, inflation, but you wouldn’t expect it to do, like, much more than that. It was literally just your saving in your house and, like, that’s what’s going on here. Not that you’re now making, like, this massive return on it, which is, I think, a function largely of housing scarcity.

But I think that, like, the thing that we’re solving here is that people right now who are literally in places where the place where they want to live for their job or family or, you know, college or whatever it is, they, like, actually can’t afford to buy in the neighborhood they’re in. And then what people are looking for is stability, not just, like, “Oh, this place I have bought, I’m stable in,” but they’re like, “This is a community I’m in. Like, I am, like, I’m a renter, I live in, you know, some city, and, like, you know, in Brooklyn or something like that, and I want to stay in my place, but I can’t afford to buy here.” So to buy is to leave the place that you are actually wanting to remain in.

And, like, there are so many stories of this, of, like — I mean, I talked to real estate agents for, for reporting all the time. And something they tell me all the time is, like, the, the number one, like, buyer’s remorse situation is when someone picks, like, amenities or some form of, like, I want this, like, house has — I need a house with three bedrooms or whatever it is, a bigger house in the suburbs that’s far away from their friends and family and community. And, like, that’s the trade-off most people have to make.

Like, if you were talking to the marginal renter right now, they can afford to rent in better neighborhoods than they can afford to buy in. And so, the trade-off is not, like, “OK, all things equal, would you rather rent or buy the home you’re in now?” It’s that given the structure of the American housing market, do you want to leave the community you’re in so you can become a homeowner? And so, that is what we’re solving.

Like, I want to really — like, that’s a lot of people who are, like, under this, like, psychic anguish and are making, I think, a bad decision to go buy a house far away from their friends and family, like, have kids without any kind of community support, and, like, whatever. And they’re like, they’re, like, dooming about it. And I’m like, you don’t have to do this.

Matthew Yglesias: But OK, but this is why I have, like, come out on the other side of the homeownership-YIMBY nexus to the view that, like, in YIMBYtopia, we’re gonna have more homeowners rather than fewer. Because, like, I agree with you, there’s a lot of people who are, like, facing this tension and they’re, like, moving into dwellings that don’t like as much in order to afford to purchase them, which is, you know, I mean, as you say, right, you have to interrogate that decision-making process, I think, a little bit more. Like, what is the purpose of, of doing something like that?

I don’t know. I mean, I, I guess where I’m landing on this is, like, I don’t — I’m not as, like, persuaded by you that this, like, a hegemonic, you know, force making people go do this. And I’m not totally sure what that...

Jerusalem Demsas: I feel like every single year of my life, my father has been like, “Why don’t you own a home?”

Matthew Yglesias: OK.

Jerusalem Demsas: Every — like, and this is not, like, unique. Like, every single one of my friends are constantly getting pressured to buy homes from, like, their family members. Like, whatever. Like, it’s just, like, I’m surprised. Maybe it’s because you grew up in New York and this was just — being a renter was much more normal. But, like, I can assure you.

Matthew Yglesias: All right, well, Mr. Demsas, if you’re out there —

Jerusalem Demsas: It’s Mr. Abraha.

Matthew Yglesias: OK.

Jerusalem Demsas: Don’t you understand Eritrean naming conventions?

Matthew Yglesias: I really don’t, no. Give Jerusalem a break, you know? She’s, like, she’s a good kid.

Jerusalem Demsas: Leave me alone.

Matthew Yglesias: She’s doing well. It’s fine.

Jerusalem Demsas: Let’s do peer review.

Matthew Yglesias: Let’s talk about some people who may or may not be doing fine.

It’s called “Fortunate Families? The Effects of Wealth on Marriage and Fertility” by David Cesarini, Erik Lindqvist, Robert Östling, and Anastasia Terskaya. It does one of my favorite things. It looks at the rich administrative data that is provided in the Nordic countries to ask what happens if you win the lottery in Sweden. And they are able to follow people for, for a number of years after winning the lottery.

And they show that men who win the lottery are more likely to get married and also have more children, whereas women who win the lottery are more likely to get divorced.

Jerusalem Demsas: In the short run.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes. Yes, right, exactly. So, it’s not like being a rich person makes you more likely to get divorced. It’s, plenty of people are like, “I’m rich now, I’m leaving,” which is funny.

And they’re — again, they’re able to show this quite rigorously because they can match not just, like, lottery winners to the general population, but they can match lottery winners to lottery players, to people who bought tickets in the exact same lottery. And so, it’s, like, a really, really good causal research design. Your dream is always to study literal lotteries about things like this.

And, these are not earth-shattering findings exactly, but they’re definitely funny.

Jerusalem Demsas: The manosphere is going to come for you now. What this paper made me think of is there was a big debate a couple years back when Melissa Kearney, who was a UMD [University of Maryland] professor, brought out her book about two-income families and Brad Wilcox had his book about getting married. The upshot of both of those books was: People should get married, it’s good for you. If you look at the average married couple, it makes them happier, better off, it’s better for their kids, etc.

And one part of this discourse that I always thought was kind of bizarre is that they kept talking about the average married couple and not the marginal married couple. And what papers like this indicate to me is, like, yeah, as a married person who’s very happy, I would bet that the average married person is happier in all these kind of ways and it’s better for them and it’s better for their kids or whatever.

But the real question is, like, if you’re trying to increase the marriage rate, we’re talking about the person who is not married right now, like, why are they not married? It’s often for, like, probably a good reason. Either they themselves are not in a place to be married or their partner is, like, not in a good place to be married.

And, like, what this indicates to me is that, like, on the margins, like, making people better off when they have the option, there are these relationships that are, like, not good that are being forced together by virtue of bad economic conditions. Not, like, people would rationally opt into marriage if they knew all of the benefits. It’s like, no, so knowing all the benefits, now having an option, like, women are like, “Get me out of here.”

Matthew Yglesias: Well...

Jerusalem Demsas: Not all women. Not all women.

Matthew Yglesias: I think this is, like, a good — this is actually, like, where I wish we would see some follow-up studies on this, because I agree, right? We’ve always, I, I don’t want to say always, but, like, this is a big question about all this marriage research is. Like, we know that married couples are better off than single people on a wide, wide range of dimensions, some financial, but, like, psychological as well.

But, of course, people are not randomly assigned to marriages, and you — and you can’t really randomly assign people to get married.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, you can. It would just be very, very bad.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, you wouldn’t be testing the hypothesis, I guess. So, I mean, it would be interesting to know, right, if you track these, you know, windfall Swedish divorcees, right? Like, what is their, you know, subjective well-being 10, 15 years down the road compared to the non-lottery winners?

Now, you would expect them to be better off in the sense that they had money. If people are being fully rational, then this, like, wealth shock-induced divorces should be, like, further enhancing their better-offness. But that’s not known per se, right?

I mean, I think, I think, like, part of the hypothesis of the marriage promotion people is that humans are underrating the value of connection, right? And that, like, part of the idea of, like — the point of the, like, for richer, for poorer, good health, bad, etc., etc., right? Is that, like —

Jerusalem Demsas: I like that it’s for poorer but not for richer.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, sure. Yes. No, but I mean, but, like, that, like, part of the issue is that, like, you are pre-committing yourself, theoretically, to staying in this partnership, even if instantaneously that is an inconvenient scenario for you. And there’s, like, a hypothesis that that’s, like, net-net, like, better for people in the long run.

Now, obviously there are limits to that, right? So, in the popular write-up of this, the way they describe this is that “wealth transfers targeted to women may enhance their bargaining power within the household and help them leave a destructive marriage.” Clearly that could be the case, right?

I do think it’s notable that we’re talking about Sweden here though, right? I mean, we’re not talking about, you know, peasant farmers in a very low-income country where there may be, like, literally no exit option, right? The, like, basic status quo in Sweden gives you some of the best exit options in terms of limiting your financial downside risk, right? Like, that’s one of the big points of having a generous welfare state.

And so, you know, it would be good to dig in to, like, to what extent is that, like, actually the thing that is happening?

Jerusalem Demsas: What is the, what is the alternative in your view?

Matthew Yglesias: That you’re just destabilizing the interpersonal dynamic in, like, some kind of way.

Jerusalem Demsas: How so? Like, now men can’t hold the, can’t hold the money above their wife’s head?

Matthew Yglesias: I mean, I don’t know what it is.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I just mean, like, even, even in Sweden, and you do see men making more money on average than their wives.

Matthew Yglesias: Absolutely. I mean, again, the male part of this is also relevant. The men who have more money, it seems like more people want to marry them because there’s some upside to that.

Jerusalem Demsas: And I mean, to be clear, the overall effect is more marriages because of what’s going on here. So even though in the short run this is what’s happening, what they find overall is more marriages.

And also, like, small but positive effects on fertility, which I think is, like — there’s, like, a real doomer take out there in the pronatalist discourse that you cannot just invest money like that. You, like, that, like, making people better off would not increase number of kids they have.

Like, I think in some ways this is, like, a rejection of this view they view as, like, kind of left-wing, like, “Oh, people aren’t having kids anymore because it’s too expensive.” They, like, hate that take because, “Well, your parents were poorer than you and they had kids.” It’s stupid. But, like, these are actually separate questions. Like, even though poorer in the past had kids at a higher rate. Right now, it is the case that there are a lot of people who, if you were giving them some money, would probably just have another kid or have their first kid.

And I think there’s, like, a — I mean, there’s now good evidence that, like, it would be a lot of money. It would probably be, like, on the order of Social Security that you would need to pay in order to get the fertility rate up to the level that would make us more comfortable. But, you know, I think this is, like, you know —

Matthew Yglesias: …yes, I agree, I agree with that. I mean, it is definitely evidence for that. But again, I mean, we, we’ve seen this in, in a number of different studies of different things, right? Like, in the fracking boom, right?

That financial windfalls that specifically skew toward men have, like, a different impact on people’s family behavior than ones that are neutral, or, in this case, ones that are skewed toward women, right?

Like, when women win the lottery, like, they don’t have more kids. They get divorced more.

Jerusalem Demsas: In the short run.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes, yes.

Jerusalem Demsas: No, but I mean, like, that’s important. In the long run, that’s not true.

Matthew Yglesias: No, I — I mean —

Jerusalem Demsas: In the short run, it’s giving them the option to leave a bad relationship.

Matthew Yglesias: I mean, I, I agree.

Jerusalem Demsas: And in the long run, they often are married at the same rate that you’d expect.

Matthew Yglesias: I, I mean, it’s just, you know, it, it’s interesting, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: It is interesting.

Matthew Yglesias: And you have, you know, so there was Jake Kozloski, who runs some, like, new dating app thing, you know, he was tweeting about his surveys, and they, like, ask people if they would marry somebody who’s less educated than them. And women are much more reluctant than men to do that. Like, less intelligent, it’s like an even bigger gap. And earns less, there’s, like, an even bigger, bigger gap there. So, you know, people have different preferences, and this seems to be shaping their choices in life.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, I mean, I would, you know, not to put on my 2017 feminism hat or whatever, but I mean, I think there’s, like, actually a — it’s very, like, clinical to, like, think marriages or matching in this, like, very economist-y way of, like, people getting together and transacting certain things. Like, women are giving this and men are giving this in heterosexual relationships and that’s how you get to a match level, right? Like, I think in the real world, like, individual people are, like, actually connecting with people on, like, a, you know, more vibes-y level.

But I think what you do see in general is that there are, like — if you think of relationships as having, you know, people bringing something to the table, in a world where women are earning their own income and are often the breadwinners of households at a much higher rate than any other generation, and they’re the ones doing most of the child rearing, and they’re the ones actually having the kids, and they’re the ones who are, like, doing all the social stuff. It sort of becomes a question of, like, would any positive shock to, like, male bargaining power do this?

So, like, if men — you could, like, randomly say, like, not just money, but, like, men just become 10% better at, like, taking care of kids, if men become, like, 30% better of, like, setting up birthday parties for their family, whatever, like, social, emotional well-being things increasing. Like, I expect you would see the exact same things here and that it wouldn’t just be, like...

Matthew Yglesias: …that would be a fun lottery.

Jerusalem Demsas: It would be a very difficult lottery. Yeah, you just are immediately imbued with the ability to, like, remember people’s birthdays and get them cards.

Matthew Yglesias: Facebook does that.

Jerusalem Demsas: Still, still difficult for people.

Matthew Yglesias: Has it transformed society?

Jerusalem Demsas: Are you still on Facebook?

Matthew Yglesias: Mostly just for the birthdays — need the birthday reminders. No, my wife reminds me when my friends’ birthdays are, even though I see it on Facebook.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, sorry Kate.

Matthew Yglesias: Sad stuff.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right, well, if you enjoyed this episode, come back next week. Subscribe, tell your friends about the show. Subscribe to The Argument, subscribe to Slow Boring, and we’ll see you next Thursday. Bye.

Reality is a Communist Plot

Of MAGA and the totalitarian mindset

Paul Krugman
Jul 30
 
READ IN APP
 

The Covid vaccine didn’t work, and vaccines cause autism. But hydroxychloroquine worked, and so did ivermectin. Anthony Fauci killed millions of people.

Climate change is a hoax. Wind power caused a massive TV blackout during the Trump-Biden debate. Solar power is useless because the sun doesn’t shine at night, and batteries don’t exist. Smoke blanketed North America, not because of climate change, but because Canada didn’t rake its 2 million square miles of boreal forest.

We’ve destroyed Iran’s military, and the Iranian regime is begging for a deal. Also, the U.S. isn’t running out of precision weapons as a result of the Iran war, and furthermore the shortage is Joe Biden’s fault.

The economy is in a “golden age.” Prices are down. And Trump has a 59 percent approval rating.

Trump won the 2020 election.

Communism is the greatest threat facing America.

The modern American right is very good at hating. MAGA hates immigrants (unless they’re white South Africans); it hates liberals; it hates scientists.

What the ongoing show trial of Fauci — which motivated this post — has really driven home, however, is that what Trump and his supporters hate most of all is reality. They know what they want to believe. They fly into paroxysms of rage whenever someone points out that the world isn’t what they want it to be. And they always want to shoot the messenger.

Of course, motivated reasoning isn’t confined to the right. Some people on the left insist that zoning restrictions have no role in causing high housing prices, that it’s all about Wall Street greed. Many centrists insist that being in the middle on a left-right scale — which isn’t even how most voters think about politics — is the secret to electoral victory. And so on.

I’m not immune to the temptation to believe what I want to be true. I try to fight it, but don’t always succeed. Still, I try to acknowledge and admit it when I have let wishful thinking warp my judgement.

But what we’re seeing now isn’t run-of-the-mill motivated reasoning. It’s something far more extreme.

If believing something suits MAGA’s prejudices and interests, they don’t hesitate: they simply insist that it’s true. They routinely dismiss scientific and statistical evidence, but they don’t stop there. They’re perfectly willing to deny reality even if the truth is staring them in the face.

Thus, Trump urged Americans to remember that 2024 TV blackout, which nobody remembers because it didn’t happen. He insists that California has “blackouts and brownouts every weekend,” when the state’s 39 million residents can tell you it doesn’t. He says that you must show ID to buy groceries, which everyone who buys their own food knows isn’t so.

Do Trump and his followers actually believe these things? As I see it, that’s a category error, starting from the presumption that they even accept that objective facts exist. All the evidence (Hah! “Evidence!”) says that they don’t.

George Orwell, whose work seems more relevant by the day, knew all about this mindset. In his essay “Looking back on the Spanish war” he wrote about how the rise of totalitarianism had changed the rules:

In the past people deliberately lied, or they unconsciously coloured what they wrote, or they struggled after the truth, well knowing that they must make many mistakes; but in each case they believed that ‘the facts’ existed and were more or less discoverable. And in practice there was always a considerable body of fact which would have been agreed to by almost everyone.

Totalitarians, however, denied that objective facts existed. Furthermore, reality is mutable, changing with the leader’s whims:

If the Leader says of such and such an event, ‘It never happened’ – well, it never happened. If he says that two and two are five – well, two and two are five.

If you find the assertion that MAGA has a totalitarian mindset over the top, all I can ask is, have you been following the news?

What’s remarkable is the extent to which Republican politicians act as if they are living in a totalitarian state, when they aren’t — not yet, anyway. ICE would clearly like to be an American Stasi, policing any deviation from the party line, but it’s not able, so far, to arrest members of Congress who express skepticism about the president’s claims. And many Republican politicians still, I believe, know the difference between fantasy and reality.

But they behave as if they were courtiers to Kim Jong Un. Trump speeches are sometimes followed by “endless applause moments,” because none of Trump’s loyalists wants to be seen as the first person to stop clapping.

The susceptibility of the GOP to this totalitarian mindset has come as a surprise even to cynics. I have some idea of how this happened: It involves a confluence of big-money corruption, crony capitalism, religious fanaticism, and the ever-present forces of racism and sexism. But that’s a subject to be delved into another day.

What’s clear is that the war on reality is exacting a high price on America as a whole.

Remember, 1.2 million Americans died from Covid — a number that would have been much lower if MAGA misinformation hadn’t caused so many people to refuse vaccination. Now we’re seeing a frightening rise in measles and other infectious diseases, and God help us if another pandemic strikes with Trump or his successor still in charge.

Climate denial and hostility to renewable energy will mean more pollution even as it consigns the U.S. to energy and economic backwardness.

And the Iran war — which Trump started and now refuses to end because he won’t accept reality — has destroyed America’s credibility and depleted our weapon stocks with stunning speed.

But anyone pointing out the obvious is, of course, a Communist.

title: Why did South Korean stocks just crash?

Why did South Korean stocks just crash?

The AI boom creates a lot of uncertainty.

Noah Smith
Jul 30
 
READ IN APP
 

Explaining stock market movements is always a little bit of a fool’s errand; no one really understands why stocks boom or crash on a given day or in a given week. Over the long run, the stock market displays lots of “excess volatility” — prices move up and down much more than is warranted by changes in earnings or other measures of fundamental value. There are plenty of theories about why those swings happen, but it’s very hard to know which of those — if any — is in operation at any given time. And so although every big stock market movement is followed by lots of articles claiming to know why, you should take them all — including this one — with several grains of salt.

Anyway, having said all that…

The Korean stock market has been crashing for weeks now. Around March, Korean stocks went on an epic tear; the KOSPI index rose from around 5,000 to over 9,000. Then, just over a month ago, it all went into reverse, with the index falling back to around 5,500:

There are probably two stories regarding why this happened — one about fundamentals, and another about finance. In fact, this is typical for bubbles and crashes, not just in stocks but in every asset class. There’s almost always some kind of connection to fundamentals — some story about how we’re in a new economy, followed by doubts about whether that story is really true, and so on. But the big market movements are almost always accelerated by purely financial factors — “noise traders” armed with piles of excess cash, opportunistic speculators looking to ride the wave of sentiment, and so on.¹

For Korea, the fundamental story was about memory stocks. Korean companies like SK Hynix and Samsung make a lot of the world’s computer memory. Under normal circumstances, computer memory isn’t a great business to be in — the technology is fairly commoditized, the industry is brutally competitive, it takes a LOT of capital to build the factories, and it’s very risky to make long-term bets on the evolution of memory technology.

But computer memory is really important for AI data centers. And so the AI boom kicked off the mother of all memory booms. Only a few companies had the scale to meet a large amount of this demand explosion, and the two biggest of these were in South Korea. SK Hynix’s operating profit went from under $10 billion in the first quarter of 2025 to over $35 billion in the first quarter of 2026:

Hynix, which specializes in memory, briefly had a higher market capitalization than Samsung, simply because the memory boom is so huge. Korea’s exports rose over 70% in just one year; in fact, the country’s whole national GDP growth rate increased by a noticeable amount over the past two quarters, just because of this one product:

That’s a pretty strong fundamental story about why South Korean stocks should be worth a lot more. So it’s no surprise that the Korean stock market boomed as soon as people realized in early 2026 that AI technology is going to be extremely valuable. Here’s a thread about just how epic the runup in these companies’ stock prices was:

The Kobeissi Letter
@KobeissiLetter
What happened? Chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung saw historic gains, rising +1,900% and +600% in one year, respectively. These two stocks accounted for as much as 50% of South Korea's stock market last month. Never in history has growth at this scale happened so quickly.
1:50 PM · Jul 29, 2026 · 163K Views
11 Replies · 62 Reposts · 1.13K Likes

This is where the financial story rears its head, though. A bunch of traders saw this enormous price rise and decided to buy into it. You’d think a lot of these would be foreign, but international investors mostly avoided the boom (except for a few who bet big on Korean memory stocks). The most frenzied buyers were regular Korean people — the proverbial taxi drivers and teenagers.

These investors probably didn’t understand the fundamental story about AI and data centers and so on. Instead, they probably had extrapolative expectations — they see the price go up and up, and they figure stocks are just a “goer upper”. As more and more buy in and the stock goes up more and more, the perception of a structural upward trend is only reinforced, causing yet more people to buy in. This isn’t the only explanation for coordinated “noise trader” buying frenzies, but it’s probably the most likely.

Normal people don’t have a lot of cash sitting around. But earlier this year, regular Korean people got the opportunity to effectively borrow lots of money to invest it in stocks, via the introduction of leveraged single-stock ETFs. When you buy a share in a leveraged single-stock ETF in SK Hynix, it’s like borrowing money to buy SK Hynix stock.

A whole lot of Koreans used leveraged ETFs and other borrowing methods to borrow huge amounts of money and buy lots and lots of Korean stocks — especially the memory company stocks that were driving everything.

There were some people selling — notably, foreign investors “taking profits” and getting out. But the noise traders overwhelmed all the selling pressure, and sent stock prices soaring.

Then something happened last month — either something fundamental or something financial. Hynix and Samsung are doing fine in terms of earnings growth, but it’s possible that something suddenly gave traders reason to doubt the overall story about the AI boom sending these companies’ profits to the moon. The other possibility is that Korea simply ran out of hotheaded day traders willing to borrow more and more in order to bet on stocks, and the influx of cash naturally came to a halt.

Whichever it was, at that point the price faltered and began to fall. All that borrowed money accelerated the fall on the way down. When prices fall, leveraged ETFs have to sell some of what they hold.² When a bunch of leveraged ETFs do this at the same time, it pushes prices down, forcing others to sell. In the meantime, people who had borrowed money to buy stock faced margin calls (or bankruptcy), forcing them to sell stock to raise cash. All of this created extra selling pressure, and so increased the rate at which Korean stock prices fell since late June.

Anyway, that’s the financial story. It’s a very old story — financial leverage plus unsophisticated new buyers plus a strong fundamental story often produces a bubble and crash, or exacerbates one that was already in progress. No wonder Korea is now moving — a little belatedly — to restrict leveraged ETFs.

But while financial factors affected the timing and the size of the stock price boom and bust, the fundamental story is more interesting. Fears of an AI bubble are quietly creeping back.

In 2025, as consumer chatbots struggled to find a market big enough to justify the kind of investments being made, there was a lot of talk about an AI bubble. One possibility was that AI revenues wouldn’t grow fast enough to justify the amount being invested in data centers. Another possibility was that AI companies wouldn’t have enough of a “moat” to make them consistently profitable.

In 2026, Claude Code exploded onto the scene, and everyone realized that AI had finally found “product-market fit”. We now know at least one thing that AI is incredibly useful for — writing computer code. Suddenly, an AI bubble seemed much less likely. Spending on AI was skyrocketing, and Anthropic — the new market leader — was successfully capturing much of the profits. Cybersecurity and other zero-sum applications — where having the absolute best model can matter a lot — started to seem like the “moat” that AI had previously lacked. Suddenly, the giant data center construction boom seemed a lot more reasonable.

But slowly, doubts have begun to creep back in. AI is amazing at writing software, but writing software is different from selling it. So far, huge increases in coding productivity are translating into only minor increases in the amount of software being shipped:

It’s possible that a significant fraction of the explosion in the use of coding agents is just “tokenmaxxing” — companies trying to use as much AI as they can, either to learn to use the tools, or perhaps just to look like they’re doing something. If so, we can expect a retrenchment and a temporary slowdown of AI spending growth.

It’s also possible that even the revenue growth we’ve seen isn’t enough to offset the enormous costs of the data center boom. Here’s a recent report from The Economist:

A back-of-the-envelope calculation finds that covering AI capex through identifiable AI income requires revenue on the order of $2.5trn per year, more than tech’s entire combined revenue today…Anthropic pulls in perhaps $75bn, annualised; OpenAI makes tens of billions; Google, via its AI model Gemini, and Microsoft probably get a bit less. SpaceX may have a few billion dollars’ worth of revenue from enterprise AI this year. Meta also makes a few bucks from AI. Add this up and you land at roughly $150bn a year. [emphasis mine]

AI revenue is growing very fast, but if these calculations are right, it’ll have to grow by 17x from where it is now in order to justify the capital being spent. In other words, even Claude Code isn’t enough; AI revenue has to accelerate even further, and while it’s perfectly plausible that it could do that, it’s a big question mark.

There’s also the possibility that the moat of companies like Anthropic is less invincible than it looked just a couple of months ago. A Chinese company called Moonshot AI has released a model called Kimi K3 that nearly equals the best available American models. American companies are using cheap Chinese AI models more and more for daily tasks. If Anthropic and OpenAI lose the overall b2b market to cheap Chinese competition — which is undoubtedly supported, of course, by China’s usual blizzard of subsidies and government supports — there’s not much chance that they’ll be able to pay for the data center boom.

And at that point, there could be a big, big bust — similar to when railroads went under in 1873. Investors are probably already beginning to worry about this. It isn’t just Korean AI-related stocks that have taken a hit recently. Here’s Nvidia, which designs and furnishes the chips that run data centers:

And here’s Micron, America’s top memory chip maker:

And here’s Microsoft, a big part of whose business is installing AI data centers:

There are similar (if less dramatic) stories at Google and Amazon, who also run a ton of data centers.

Here’s Bloomberg’s story about the decline of the so-called “Magnificent 7” tech stocks:

Wall Street is growing increasingly concerned about the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech is spending on artificial intelligence…“The real problem is the amount of spend that’s going on,” said Ken Mahoney, chief executive officer of Mahoney Asset Management. “No one knows what the return on investment is.”…The selloff is coming as investors grow increasingly cautious about the massive sums that Big Tech firms are spending to build out their AI infrastructure. The Mag 7 index is now down 11% from a record reached in late May, erasing $2 trillion in market value.

So although South Korea’s epic stock crash was probably related to Korea-specific financial factors, it could also herald the return of the “AI bubble” story. AI is far and away the most important thing going on in the American economy right now, so any hint of a bubble is worrying.

How Trump made America less popular than China

Speak loudly and blunder a lot

Matthew Yglesias
Jul 30
 
READ IN APP
 

There’s more to foreign policy than being liked, but part of being a great power is dealing with the choice lesser powers face between bandwagoning with a strong country and counterbalancing against it.

For a long time, most observers have seen this as an underlying American advantage vis-a-vis China. Many countries that are geographically near the People’s Republic — notably Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan — have expressed a strong and clear preference for an alliance with the United States of America in a way that has absolutely no counterpart among America’s neighbors. Even countries, like Vietnam, whose historical relationship with the United States was quite negative seem to prefer aligning with a distant and relatively benevolent United States to being under the Chinese Communist Party’s thumb.

But things have taken a pretty sharp turn lately. In Pew polling from earlier this summer, China is now viewed more favorably than the United States in a wide range of countries, including Mexico and Canada and most major European countries.

Some of this seems like polarization around Israel, with Israel itself expressing the most favorable views of the United States and a number of Muslim countries exhibiting the biggest gap in China’s favor.

But beyond the specifics of that conflict, I think this reflects the wider implications of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran.

The higher energy costs brought about by the war have been extremely unpopular domestically. But the economic impact abroad has been worse than the impact at home, and people globally are justifiably angry that as much as Trump has screwed his own constituents on this, he’s inflicted even more pain on them.

And then there’s the bizarre “bad neighbor policy” that has characterized Trump’s second term. Trump transformed Canadian politics with pointless threats to invade the country. He’s got European governments wargaming a fight with the United States over Greenland. Every few months he muses about invading Mexico to fight drug cartels.

None of this stuff is popular with American voters, but it’s also remote from their key concerns, so it gets less attention than purely domestic concerns.

Yet in terms of the long-term harm done to the country, torching America’s reputation with friendly countries for the sake of what mostly amounts to a gag should count among the worst of the Orange Man’s actions.

Subscribed

The anti-Roosevelt doctrine

Teddy Roosevelt articulated the view that the United States ought to “speak softly and carry a big stick,” letting the objective realities of American power speak for themselves while presenting a friendly face to the world.

Trump has done something like the reverse, engaging in maximum bluster while in practice having little interest in anything other than personal corruption and his White House ballroom.

That’s how we end up in bizarre situations like a feud with the government of Italy that started with him bragging for no reason that Giorgia Meloni “begged” him for a bilateral photo op. There’s no actual dispute between the United States and Italy, no real conflict of interest, and Meloni and Trump are pretty like-minded in their approach to domestic politics. Trump is just a jerk who seems like he has trouble with women and never wants to apologize for anything.

Trump is funnier and more entertaining than the average politician — there’s a reason he was a successful reality-television host. And even though becoming president is more impressive than hosting “The Apprentice,” there’s a strong case that the ratings of “The Apprentice” relative to other shows were a good deal more impressive than his approval ratings relative to other presidents.

I think this is why he gets really into these bits like calling Justin Trudeau “governor” of Canada or dispatching JD Vance to Greenland. I’d like to say in a very serious tone of voice, “But there’s nothing funny about the central pillar of the Western alliance acting like a petty bully.” In truth, though, it is kind of funny — it’s just also really bad.

Different jobs come with different responsibilities, and one of the responsibilities of the job of being president is to act in a dignified and appropriate manner, not provoke international incidents for the lulz.

The price of war

Something Trump does not seem to have considered is that some leaders take their jobs more seriously than he does.

After the audacious gambit in Venezuela paid off, Trump seems to have convinced himself that every regime is as hollow and corrupt as Maduro’s. He figured that after he killed a few top guys, whoever was left in Iran would cut a deal. That didn’t work, and he’s been floundering ever since.

The ensuing war has been a big deal for Trump politically because it has pushed up the cost of energy in a way that infuriates voters.

Notably, though, the United States is a net exporter of oil and oil products. So while the supply shock is still on balance bad for the American economy, it really is a balance. Increased domestic production and energy income partially offset the harm of higher prices and mean that the impact on the American economy is much milder than the impact on countries that import all or most of their oil.

With natural gas, we’re even more insulated. There are physical limits to how much gas can be exported from the United States because only so many liquefaction facilities exist. As a result, there are basically two separate gas prices: the price of gas that can be obtained via pipeline from American fields and the higher global price of liquefied gas shipped by sea. Limited pipeline capacity in the Northeast means that New England relies on seaborne gas and has to pay the global price. But most Americans are basically protected from the supply disruption.

Trump periodically tries to make this point, arguing that “we don’t need the Hormuz Strait” because the United States does not import oil and gas from the Middle East.

That’s not quite right. The global price of oil still influences American prices, and the global price of gas influences prices in part of the country. But he is correct that the price Americans are paying is much lower than the price being paid by people in Thailand or the Bahamas.

What Trump doesn’t quite seem to grasp is that this makes his policy look much worse.

Subscribed

After all, Americans are incredibly angry about what this war is doing to their pocketbooks and their economy, and Trump is correct to say that other people are suffering much more dramatically than we are. That’s real rogue superpower behavior. You’re sitting around in Chile or Bangladesh and, out of nowhere, your economy is being ravaged by some shit the American government started that you had no say in, and the president is actually bragging about how he’s better off than you.

The helpful Chinese

One point in the hawks’ favor is that global oil prices have actually spiked less than most observers (myself included) initially assumed they would.

It seemed like reducing global oil consumption by enough to make up for the lost output would require world prices well over $100 per barrel on a sustained basis. Why hasn’t that happened?

Well, China has dramatically cut oil imports, single-handedly absorbing 74 percent of the total global reduction in imports through a mix of rationing and drawing down its existing stockpiles. The Chinese government is a repressive autocratic regime, and so we never get really clear reporting on exactly what their thinking is. They surely have their own reasons for reacting this way. But the upshot is that while the United States has inflicted great economic harm on various countries around the world, China’s extraordinary steps have limited the harm to much less than initially expected.

So you have Trump picking pointless fights and making people mad for no reason and then plunging the world into a dire economic situation. Meanwhile, China is actually taking constructive action to improve things.

China has also been flooding the world with what seem to be affordable, high-quality electric cars, which is good for the environment and for the economic health of oil-importing countries. I’ve defended the logic of the Biden and Trump administrations’ efforts to keep these cars out and prevent China from totally dominating the global automobile supply chain.

But to pull this off — or to achieve the comparable goal of preventing Chinese companies from dominating artificial intelligence — we need other countries to cooperate with us.

And that won’t happen if the United States is slapping tariffs on everyone left and right in a totally unprincipled way. It’s not a remotely compelling pitch!

Trump mostly makes America look like a joke, but to the extent that we are not a joke — and certainly our frontier A.I. labs are no laughing matter — he’s made American primacy look alarming to the point where few countries welcome it and a majority seem to prefer our rival.

This is, rightly, not what Democrats are going to be campaigning on this fall. But on the merits, it’s easily one of Trump’s most egregious failures.

The Bond Market Doesn’t Like Bullshit

Why Kevin Warsh just bombed

Paul Krugman
Jul 31
 
READ IN APP
 

CNBC

The Federal Open Market Committee of the Federal Reserve meets every eight weeks to set interest rates — specifically the federal funds rate, the overnight rate at which banks lend each other money. The Fed funds rate has little direct economic significance, since nobody making important investments relies on overnight money. But an upward or downward change in the Fed funds rate tends to drag longer-term rates up or down with it. Even more important, FOMC decisions, along with their public statements, affect the market’s expectations about future monetary policy.

Setting such expectations is one of the major roles of the Fed. So FOMC decision days are something of a theatrical performance. The committee doesn’t just announce its interest rate decision. It releases a statement explaining that decision; then the Fed chair holds a press conference, in which he or she tries to build credibility by answering reporters’ questions. Market traders closely analyze these statements in order to predict the future direction of inflation and monetary policy. As a result, FOMC decisions and statements have critical influence over current market rates.

On Wednesday Kevin Warsh, who Donald Trump selected as Fed chair, played the starring role. His job was to explain why the Fed didn’t raise rates in the face of inflation that is persistently well above its 2 percent target.

By all accounts he bombed. In particular, the bond market, the ultimate reviewer, really didn’t like Warsh’s performance. As the chart at the top of this post shows, the 30-year Treasury rate spiked and the dollar fell slightly. In plain English, this was the equivalent of bond market traders running for the exits.

A little background is in order to understand exactly what happened here. At 3.7%, inflation has been persistently well over the Fed’s 2% target rate — largely as a consequence of Trump’s tariffs, which have raised the prices of imports, and his Iran war, which has caused energy prices to soar. The Fed normally raises interest rates to fight inflation. But it instead left rates on hold in this meeting.

The truth is that the case for an immediate rate hike was somewhat iffy. When a spike in inflation is temporary and will soon fade away from its own accord, the Fed tries to “look through” this temporary shock and not base interest rate decisions on it. Both the Trump tariffs and the energy price spikes are arguably one-time events. But whether the inflation shock is truly transitory is not certain. Thus three of the FOMC’s 12 members dissented and called for a small rate hike. And it’s important to note that three dissents is a lot. This was the first time since 1970 that a new Fed chair faced three opponents to an early interest rate decision. Yet Wednesday’s decision not to increase the federal funds rate was widely expected, and shouldn’t have rattled markets.

But the bond market was indeed rattled. Its reaction indicated that traders believe that there is a good chance that the Fed is going to keep rates too low for too long and thereby feed inflation. As a result, the Fed will eventually be forced to raise future rates to a higher level than if it acted to rein in inflation now.

So it’s clear that the bond market reaction wasn’t a judgment on the rate decision itself. It was, instead, a judgment on Warsh. In other words, Warsh’s remarks on Wednesday led the market to distrust his commitment to fighting inflation.

When Trump selected Warsh, I noted that Warsh had been completely wrong about monetary policy in the aftermath of the financial crisis. He called for rate hikes, which was the exactly wrong policy for a deeply depressed economy. He warned about inflation; when the inflation didn’t materialize, he just came up with new arguments for the same policies. I didn’t mince words about the consequences of choosing Warsh as Fed chair:

Many media reports are describing Warsh as a monetary hawk. That’s a category error. Warsh is a political animal. He calls for tight money and opposes any attempt to boost the economy when Democrats hold the White House. Like all Trumpers, he has been all for lower interest rates since November 2024.

As I pointed out at the time, other independent economists had similar things to say. So how did he end up at the top of the Fed? As I noted,

[Warsh is] an effective bullshitter. Sorry for the technical language, but I can’t find another way to say it. Listen to Warsh on economic policy, and he throws around a lot of big words that presumably sound impressive to people who don’t know anything about the subject. But there’s no coherent argument behind the verbiage.

What Warsh really needed to do in his press conference was refute the critics and show that he was more than a partisan who got the job in part because Trump thinks he looks the part. He failed.

Warsh didn’t necessarily need to advocate a rate hike. But he has harshly denounced the Fed for acting too slowly to tame inflation in the Biden years. Now he finds himself in a superficially similar situation, so at the very least he needed to explain clearly why he thinks this time is different. Instead, his performance at the press conference was stumbling, confusing, and evasive. At times he seemed to suggest that the Fed doesn’t need to do anything to control inflation, a total contradiction of his previous critiques.

Scattered reports also suggest that Warsh is failing to gain the respect of his colleagues at the Fed. Three dissents is, as I said, a lot. One Fed governor, Chris Waller, mocked Warsh’s plans to set up multiple task forces to study key issues. According to the Wall Street Journal,

What’s the point of all this, [Warsh] asked. Tell me who you’re putting on these groups, he said, and I’ll tell you what they’ll say. There were no brilliant ideas out there that everyone had somehow missed.

And Lorie Logan, the president of the Dallas Fed, made a point of concluding a recent speech by reminding the audience that

Neither I nor any other single person makes monetary policy on their own in the United States. The Federal Open Market Committee is a committee.

Whatever she meant by that, the audience surely heard it as saying, “Don’t worry, Warsh isn’t really in charge.” That’s reassuring if one doesn’t trust his judgment, but it also means that he won’t be an effective leader if we face an economic crisis.

Now, Warsh isn’t Trump’s worst appointment, by a long shot. Even among the economic appointments, he’s nowhere near the depths of corrupt sycophancy plumbed by Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, and Howard Lutnick, the Commerce secretary.

But the markets were looking for some sign that Warsh isn’t the lightweight bullshitter he appears to be. What they got instead was evidence that Warsh is no better than he seems. And let’s hope to God we don’t have another economic crisis while he is at the helm.

Plus N.B.A. analytics, the Paramount deal, and the dream of stronger political parties

Matthew Yglesias

Not to just make this Matt’s Grievance Corner, but recently Natalie Winters published a Twitter thread starting with the line “REVEALED: Here Are the Mainstream Journalists on China’s Payroll” that goes on to name me as one of the journalists in question.

The actual allegation here turns out to be that I took a trip to China in 2009 that was paid for by an entity with links to the Chinese government. This is not what being “on China’s payroll” means. It’s also not a new revelation — the exact same documents were written up five years ago. But also I wrote about this trip at the time! It was not a secret and has never been a secret and has never involved any kind of ongoing relationship. More to the point, the reason you can know this trip is not the secret corrupt reason for my pro-P.R.C. views is that I don’t have pro-P.R.C. views. Winters’s thread includes examples of the allegedly soft on China things that people who went on these tours said, and her one for me is that I made fun of how clumsy the propaganda we were subjected to was.

Natalie Winters
@nataliegwinters
Matthew Yglesias joked about wanting to “give Party flunkies notes” on improving their “propaganda.” Ezra Klein later credited China with buying America time during COVID.
3:21 PM · Jul 27, 2026 · 113K Views
14 Replies · 781 Reposts · 4.72K Likes

I wrote a whole book about my dream of re-aligning American politics from top to bottom around geopolitical competition with China. I’ve complained that despite his rhetoric, Trump has failed to engage seriously in competition and instead has gone soft on export controls. My opinions about this are not some big secret.

Esang Wu: Your comment about Tisch and Mamdani’s good working relationship made me curious how long do you think it lasts and why do you think it has sustained so far? I have my own guess having listened to Rahm Emanuel describe having breakfast with Mamdani after the primary. Apparently Rahm tried confronting him at the end of the meeting over not accepting Israel as a Jewish state and all but he said Mamdani was receptive, doesn’t really argue like that or didn’t want to argue about it and made him feel heard even though it was clear he hadn’t changed his mind. My takeaway seems to be that Mamdani is very disarming interpersonally, avoids bringing up conflict topics, isn’t argumentative and is looking to find common ground. But you said somewhere you went to school with Tisch, so what’s your read of their dynamic?

Jessica Tisch and I were in the same class in high school and then went to college together, so while I can’t claim we were close friends or anything, I did know her because we were in the same advanced-track science classes and such. But that was a long time ago. And I have to say that at the time nobody was writing her in as “Most Likely to Become N.Y.P.D. Commissioner.”

Her life and career ended up on an unexpected trajectory that I actually think is notable and praiseworthy. She’s from a very rich family and while there are a lot of kids who grow up in those circumstances and want to commit themselves to something high-minded, very few of them express that by rolling up their sleeves to actually do public sector work, as Tisch has.

That’s just all to say that it was a long time ago and I can’t claim any special insights into her current thinking. But I do think there are a few things in their working relationship worth noting.

Zohran Mamdani has clearly decided that a strong record on crime is key to his larger project and that he more or less trusts her to deliver that. And she is happy to stay in her lane as long as she can do her job in a way that she thinks is appropriate. I very strongly doubt that they see eye to eye on Israel, but that’s not the police commissioner’s job and in fact it’s not the mayor’s job either and there’s something eccentric about how central it is to Mamdani’s personal politics. From the standpoint of the city, though, it’s much better for the mayor to have an extreme view on Israel than an extreme view on crime and policing. I think it is broadly distressing to Jewish Americans, including and in some ways especially including Jewish Americans who (like Rahm Emanuel) enthusiastically sided with Obama over Netanyahu in their clashes about settlements and Iran, that the new vibe in progressive politics is that to be a member of the team in good standing you need to swallow Palestinian nationalist narratives about the conflict whole hog. But this is not actually relevant to the governance of the city, and the latest big announcement Mamdani made about this was in fact him acknowledging that reality.

And that’s the foundation of a good working relationship. Trying to have the N.Y.P.D. enforce International Criminal Court warrants when there is no basis in American or New York law for doing so would be absurd and unprofessional and he’s not doing it — instead, the cops are doing gun seizures like they’re supposed to.

Mar02e: In the comments section of your article about the Odyssey, someone mentioned that they find it interesting that this big cultural moment is happening one week after your article about how we miss big cultural moments.

It got me to thinking -—are we experiencing a vibe shift back toward big cultural moments? I feel like we kind of are, at least compared to pre-COVID. I’d say Barbenheimer and the Eras Tour kicked it off, and then we’re also seeing pretty much all major sports events have record-breaking audiences - the NFL stopped its brief decline/flattening and just got even bigger; the World Cup was huge; the finale of the World Series and NBA finals got massive ratings. Caitlin Clark’s college finale was even a bit of a ‘cultural event.’ And then there’s been a number of blockbuster films outside of the MCU, certainly moreso than we’d had in a while.

Do you think this is a real trend? If so, what might be driving it?

I think the trend you are pointing to is both real and welcome, but it’s not really a reversal of the decline of monoculture so much as it is the residue of what’s left behind as the monoculture dissolves.

The reason that in my piece I dwelled so much on stuff like “The Single Guy” and “Suddenly Susan” is that the connective tissue of mass culture was things that were banal rather than extraordinary. When I wrote the piece, I looked up some clips of “The Single Guy” on YouTube, which got me algorithmically served some additional YouTube content focused on 1990s sitcoms. That reminded me of shows like “Wings” and “Mad About You” that were more successful and better-regarded at the time than the stuff I mentioned but that also ended up not retaining the kind of staying power of “Friends” or “Seinfeld.”

A lot of movies were big widely seen hits without being “Odyssey”-scale events. That’s because back then a lot of people were in the habit of going to the movies on any given weekend. There were, of course, lots of small little-seen independent films. And there were box office bombs. But a famous movie star could “open” a movie — i.e., get a bunch of people to go see it on opening weekend — and if the reviews and word of mouth were okay, it would end up being widely seen.

Similarly, without obtaining anything remotely resembling Taylor Swift’s level of fame and success you could have a song that was a big hit on MTV and the radio and everyone would know it. It’s not that the “one-hit wonder” as a cultural phenomenon was so amazing but the fact that it could even happen was indicative of a time when routine pop culture was just much broader in its reach. If you’re the right age, you know the Marcy Playground song “Sex and Candy” even if you (like me) have never heard another Marcy Playground song. I don’t think mass culture in that sense will come back or even could come back, because the technological substrate just doesn’t exist anymore.

What does seem to be true is that in the wake of total fragmentation, this kind of mega-event is popping up. It’s fun to participate in things with other people, so once an event starts to look like a rare shared cultural moment, there is almost a frenzy around it. I welcome that as an alternative to total atomization. But it’s not the same thing as the old world where you could take for granted that the majority of the content you consumed was also being seen or heard by a large minority of the population.

A New Jerusalem: You’ve previously written about how the left escaped the “velvet pen” (I think that was your term I can’t remember though) during Obama’s second term, with all sorts of implications for the next 3 terms. Do you think a similar thing could happen in the back half of Trump’s second administration? Will anti-abortion advocates, for example, begin defying him and demand much clearer litmus tests for republicans in the 2028 primary?

It was called the “veal pen,” and I think this is the biggest known unknown about the Republican Party and 2028. There’s a ton of furious speculation right now about JD Vance or Marco Rubio, but I think the personalities are much less significant than this dynamic.

Does someone — maybe someone way more obscure than Vance or Rubio — start getting attention on social media by calling for Republicans to actually take action to prevent the legalized killing of innocent unborn children? And if that person does start gaining traction, does that put pressure on whoever Trump endorses as his heir to start making promises in this regard? Immigration is another possible angle. Trump has obviously been taking some pretty dramatic measures on immigration. But he’s also made it cheaper for farmers to hire workers through agricultural guest-worker visas, and some Republicans in Congress are acting at the behest of the farm lobby to push for further expansion of the program. I wouldn’t expect to see anyone explicitly criticize Trump from the right on immigration, but it’s easy to imagine an even more hardcore restrictionist campaign tapping into hostility to guest workers of both the agricultural and H-1B varieties.

Trump has been a very imperfect political leader and he privately loses fights with Congress all the time. But because he so thoroughly dominates Republican politics in public, no Republican politician feels free to campaign against him or to distinguish themselves by criticizing his policies. That particular dominance presumably won’t last, but it’s not obvious what will follow it. You certainly could get something that resembles the 2016/2020 leftward rushes that happened in Democratic primaries — and the 2016 precedent is a reminder that this can happen even if a single frontrunner dominates the whole time.

Share

andrew schein: Jaylen Brown. What’s the deal with his poor advanced stats? Is it a sign he’s overrated, or that the advanced stats have problems, or a bit of both?

I think that people think I’m the kind of basketball fan who’d be super into advanced stats, but I’m actually not, or at least historically have not been. The thing that actually did get me interested in this was the sheer volume of incomprehension about the trade that came from Bill Simmons and other people in the N.B.A. media. They all said they were aware that advanced stats say Brown was nowhere near the kind of player who deserved to be sixth in M.V.P. voting but then didn’t engage at all with this question. I’m not saying people should necessarily agree with the advanced stats take, but if you’re going to spend weeks talking about how mad you are at the trade and going “What was the front office thinking?” it seems actually worth taking a moment to sit with the fact that clearly part of what the front office was thinking was that the advanced stats were right that Brown to Paul George is not that big of a downgrade.

So what do these stats mean?

I’m a Knicks fan. I fire up DARKO, and I see the take that Jalen Brunson is only the third-best player on the team.

That just does violence not only to the “eyeball test” of player quality but really also to the whole way people use language when describing N.B.A. teams. Brunson is just clearly the signature star of the team, the hero of the city, the guy who has the ball in his hands in the most critical moments. You can’t even dispute those facts, so what is the math even saying?

Here’s what I talked myself into. Suppose you’re Mike Brown and you’re told that your eight-man rotation is going to be Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns, O.G. Anunoby, and then clones of those guys. What clones do you order up? Well it’d probably be just one Brunson clone, and Brunson2’s job would be to back up Brunson when Brunson needs rest or is in foul trouble. Without appealing to any advanced stats concepts, it would just not be very promising to play a Brunson-Brunson backcourt. It would be defensively weak and the offensive contributions would be redundant. How about Towns? You’d definitely want one Towns clone so that Towns2 could back up Towns. Would you consider playing a Towns-Towns twin-towers lineup? That’s intriguing. I would definitely want one Towns clone and would consider ordering two.

With Anunoby, though, I would want a bunch. I’m very comfortable with the idea of Towns-Anunoby-Anunoby2-Anunoby3-Brunson as a five-man lineup. And then Anunoby4 coming off the bench to back those guys up sounds great. So most likely my ideal eight-man rotation is two Brunsons, two Townses, and four Anunobys. If I got a ninth guy, it would be another Towns. That aligns with the DARKO take that Anunoby > Towns > Brunson, but I think it also just aligns with an intuitive “guy who watches the games” take on how the team works. Anunoby is not the star of the team. He’s not Captain Clutch. But you can almost never have enough guys who can defend multiple positions effectively while scoring efficiently, whereas a team wants at most one undersized guard who’s a subpar defender but scores at high volume.

Max Haas: In the 2016 democratic primary, I remember a debate moment about climate change where Hillary suggested progressive climate regulations, Bernie talked about how corporations were hurting the environment, and then Martin O’Malley gave an answer where he rejected that sort of framing and then spoke about how green energy is an entrepreneurial opportunity for America. Do we need to give O’Malley way more flowers?

You guys know that O’Malley Would’ve Won is one of my core beliefs. But my recollection of the campaign is that there was some tension between the way O’Malley wanted to talk about the issue (which was generally solid) and his specific policy commitments, which largely leaned toward trying to outflank everyone as the maximal anti-pipeline candidate.

Earlier in his career, though, O’Malley was on the correct side of an interesting energy policy dispute when he tried to get a third reactor built at the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant.

Calvert Cliffs is a big facility that generates 40 percent of Maryland’s power and is far and away the state’s largest source of clean energy. The site is large enough to accommodate an additional reactor, which would significantly increase output and have all the associated benefits. And the French utility company Électricité de France was ready to go on the project when the Obama-era Nuclear Regulatory Commission stepped in to deny them permission on the grounds that it would be a national security risk to have a French company involved in the American nuclear industry.

This seems like an absurd viewpoint. France is a NATO treaty ally and a nuclear-weapon state recognized under the Non-Proliferation Treaty. What is the risk here? France is a country that knows how to build and operate a large nuclear fleet and the United States should welcome efforts to partner with it.

I am always eager to defend Obama and his administration from various progressive slanders, but his stewardship of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission was genuinely bad. The first chair he appointed came out of Harry Reid’s operation and was basically put forward just because Reid wanted someone who would stop Yucca Mountain by any means necessary. In practice, that meant picking someone who was broadly anti-nuclear and was happy to throw whatever wrenches into the works he could find.

Ant Breach: Should Andy Burnham drill in the North Sea?

Yes.

Eric H: Do you see much / any live theater? And, do you have a take on proshots (professionally-produced filmed versions of shows)?

I live right by the Studio Theatre in D.C. and it’s been almost 20 years since I attended, so basically, no, I am not a live theater fan. I did listen to a lot of Broadway musicals on tape while driving in the car when I was a kid and have affection for those — I even dragged Kate to see a revival of the “Pajama Game” in the West End when we were in London years ago.

As someone who loves movies but finds live theater a little weird, I find the proshots concept sort of doubly weird — make a real movie! Steven Spielberg’s remake of “West Side Story” is incredibly underrated in my view and shows what can happen when you marry a stage musical that people love to real cinematic craft. I would love to see a film adaptation of “Hamilton,” for example. But people just filming a play? I dunno.

Brendan: I wondered what you thought of this take from David Frum regarding the recent supreme court decision striking down limits on election spending by political parties.

Do you feel any optimism that this will bring balance to the forces pressuring Democratic candidates?

Frum is arguing that America made a mistake by financially disempowering formal party organizations. I used to be very enamored of this take, which you can find in a 2015 book on campaign finance by Ray La Raja and Brian Schaffner, but I’m now pretty sure that it’s wrong.

Their thesis was that if money flowed through institutional political parties, sober-minded professionals who are motivated to win would control the levers of power. La Raja and Schaffner believed that disintermediating the parties had allowed expressive donors to wield undue political influence, leading to extremism and polarization.

I think there are two problems with this.

One problem, as my friends Sam Rosenfeld and Daniel Schlozman argue in their newer book, “The Hollow Parties,” is that institutional political parties lack not just money but, more importantly, social, cultural, and political legitimacy. Haley Stevens’s problem in Michigan is not that she lacks access to money. It’s that a large share of Democrats — and seemingly a majority of media influencers — sincerely believe that Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren have a better track record of political judgement than Chuck Schumer and Gretchen Whitmer. I think both Schumer and Whitmer have shown real flaws in their track records but that this is still an insane assessment.

The second problem, which in my opinion is more damaging for the thesis, is that patronage machine politics doesn’t exist anymore. Many good things happened for the people of Louisiana as a result of John Bel Edwards’s two terms as governor, but it’s not like the leaders of the Louisiana Democratic Party reaped some kind of financial windfall that other state party leaders were jealous of. These are not “bosses” with a concrete stake in winning. They’re the same expressive amateurs who exist in every other part of the political system. When Charlie Baker was governor of Massachusetts, the state party institutions ended up getting taken over by MAGA-aligned true believers who didn’t like him. So I think the idea that empowering formal party organizations will empower winning-oriented pragmatists is empirically wrong.

I’m not sure exactly what the solution is. But I do think part of the answer needs to be some self-reflection on Schumer’s part. On the one hand, I believe that much of the criticism he has taken has been unfair. And I further believe that his most vociferous critics have ideas that are on the whole worse than his. That said, a party leader needs to be able to lead effectively. Throughout the 2021–22 legislative session, Schumer seemed unable or unwilling to impose priorities on his caucus. In the 2026 election cycle, it’s not just that he can’t impose his preferred candidates on key races (no leader has ever been that strong). It’s that having his support seems to be more hindrance than help. He has a large bloc of his caucus actively campaigning against his preferred candidate in Michigan and nobody flying in from out of state to help her out. This doesn’t really strike me as a tenable situation. Politics isn’t always about leaders getting what they deserve; it’s about putting the right people in the right place at the right time, and he doesn’t seem to me to be that guy.

Niketas: What are your latest thoughts on the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros merger? Bad because Ellisons/Bari Weiss/MAGA? Good for Star Trek? Bad because CBS and CNN would be merged? Good because Paramount is otherwise in trouble and a bit crap/Warner also in trouble (similar to a Sprint-TMobile argument)? Thanks!

I’ve got three basic takes on this right now. (1) CNN falling into the hands of a regime-aligned billionaire is definitely bad for America. (2) I am skeptical that there is a bona fide competition problem on the film and television production side of this deal.

And (3) there’s a reasonable argument that Paramount taking over is better for the movie business — and for cinema as an art form — than Netflix taking over would have been. Whatever else you may say about him, David Ellison seems like a guy who really wants to run a movie studio, whereas Netflix has a pretty mixed relationship to the whole concept of movies.
